title: LLM apps: prompt design, streaming, caching
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: System prompts, few-shot examples, prompt versioning, streaming to the client with SSE, exact and semantic caching, prompt caching and token budgets.
source: OpenAI prompt caching guide; Anthropic prompt caching docs (minimums, 0.1x reads, 1.25x writes); Spring Framework SseEmitter docs; FastAPI StreamingResponse docs; LangChain caching docs; OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications

questions.prompt: Your input budget is 1,000 tokens. The system prompt uses 300 tokens, the user's question uses 80 tokens, and each few-shot example costs 120 tokens. What is the maximum number of whole examples you can include?
questions.explanation: Free space is 1,000 - 300 - 80 = 620 tokens. 620 / 120 = 5.17, so 5 examples (600 tokens). More examples also raise cost and latency on every call, so pick the fewest that fix the failure.

questions.prompt: A 10,000-token stable prefix is sent in 11 calls. The first call pays the full input price for the prefix; the other 10 hit the prompt cache and pay 10% of the normal price for those tokens. Counting only the prefix, the total bill equals how many full-price prefixes?
questions.explanation: 1 full-price call + 10 x 0.10 = 2 full-price prefixes, compared with 11 without caching. Some providers also charge a premium for the cache write, which this simplified model ignores.

questions.prompt: Users send 500 requests in a day made up of 100 distinct questions, each asked exactly 5 times with identical text, model and parameters. An exact-match cache is empty at the start. How many LLM calls are made?
questions.explanation: The first occurrence of each distinct key is a miss (100 calls); the other 4 x 100 = 400 are hits. Exact caches only work when the full key (normalised text, model, temperature) matches, so real hit rates are lower than this idealised case.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: Placing the stable instructions and examples first and the variable user text last increases prompt-cache hits.
questions.reason: Prompt caching reuses work only for an identical leading prefix of the prompt.

whys.a: Right: any change early in the prompt invalidates everything after it, so stable content belongs first.
whys.b: R is exactly why A holds, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Both OpenAI (automatic, for long prompts) and Anthropic (explicit cache_control breakpoints) match on prefixes. Putting a timestamp or user id at the top of the system prompt silently kills the cache.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: A semantic cache with a very low similarity threshold, such as 0.5, is safe to run in production.
questions.reason: A semantic cache returns a stored answer when the embedding of a new query is close enough to an earlier query.

whys.a: A is false, so a is wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is false: a loose threshold returns wrong answers for different questions that merely look alike. R is true and describes the mechanism.

questions.explanation: Tune the threshold on real traffic, scope the cache per tenant and per prompt version, and never cache answers that depend on user-specific data. A false hit is a correctness bug, not just a miss.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: Streaming tokens to the client reduces perceived latency without changing the total generation time.
questions.reason: The server generates the entire answer before it sends the first byte when streaming.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: A is true (the user sees text after the first token); R is false because streaming forwards tokens as they are produced.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Time to first token is what the user feels. Streaming also lets you cancel early when the client disconnects, which saves tokens.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: Production prompts should be stored with a version id and changed through review, like code.
questions.reason: Model output is non-deterministic, so prompt changes should be checked against a fixed evaluation set with scored criteria.

whys.a: R supports a different point (testing), not the need for version ids.
whys.b: Both are true: versioning gives traceability, evals give regression safety, and they are complementary rather than causal.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Log the prompt version in every trace so a quality drop can be tied to a change. Keep the eval set small but representative, and include past failures.

questions.prompt: Match each stack with the construct normally used to stream LLM output.

left.text: Spring WebFlux or Spring AI chat client

right.text: EventSource or fetch with a ReadableStream

questions.explanation: All of them push chunks as they are produced. A fixed Content-Length body cannot stream. Spring AI exposes stream().content() on ChatClient, and LangChain4j 1.x uses StreamingChatModel with a response handler.

questions.text: A prompt cache matches an identical {1}, so stable content goes first. Anthropic marks a breakpoint with {2}, while OpenAI caches automatically once the prompt reaches {3} tokens.
questions.explanation: Anthropic: cache_control {"type": "ephemeral"} on a content block (up to 4 explicit breakpoints per request). OpenAI: automatic for prompts of 1,024 tokens or more, hits in 128-token steps. Anthropic's minimum cacheable length differs by model (from 512 to 4,096 tokens in the current docs) and shorter prompts are simply not cached, with no error, so check cache_read_input_tokens.

questions.prompt: Complete the Server-Sent Events wire format.
questions.text: An SSE response uses the media type {1}, and each event is written as 'data: ...' followed by a {2} line.
questions.explanation: SSE events are separated by an empty line. Do not confuse it with newline-delimited JSON, which is a different convention.

questions.prompt: FastAPI: an async iterator function llm_tokens(q) yields text tokens. Write an async generator gen(q) that yields each token as an SSE event ('data: <token>' plus a blank line), and a GET /chat endpoint chat(q: str) that returns it as a StreamingResponse with the SSE media type.

checks.label: uses an async generator (async def with yield)
iterates with async for over llm_tokens

questions.explanation: Other valid forms exist (a nested generator, EventSourceResponse from sse-starlette). In production also stop generating when the client disconnects.

questions.prompt: Spring MVC: write the body of a controller method SseEmitter chat(String q) that creates an emitter with no timeout, sends the text hello from a background executor (variable executor), completes the emitter, and returns it.
questions.explanation: The servlet thread returns immediately and the executor writes events. A timeout of 0L means no timeout. Returning a Flux<String> with produces = TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE is the reactive alternative.

questions.prompt: In LangChain Python, enable an in-memory exact-match cache for all LLM calls (imports included).
questions.model:
from langchain_core.globals import set_llm_cache
from langchain_core.caches import InMemoryCache

set_llm_cache(InMemoryCache())
questions.explanation: I ran this: the second identical invoke returns the cached answer without calling the model. For multi-process production use Redis- or SQL-backed caches. The older langchain.globals import path also works.

questions.prompt: Which practice best supports safe prompt changes in a production LLM service?

options.text: Keep prompts in versioned storage, tag each trace with the prompt version and run an eval set before rollout.
options.why: Right: this gives traceability and a regression gate.

options.text: Edit the system prompt string directly in production whenever quality seems to drop, then restart the service to apply it.
options.why: No history and no test, so you cannot tell if a change helped or hurt anything.

options.text: Never change prompts after launch, because any change makes the whole application behaviour unpredictable.
options.why: Prompts need tuning; the answer is controlled change, not freezing them forever.

options.text: Store prompts only inside each developer's local notebooks and share the winning text over chat messages.
options.why: Not reproducible and not auditable, and the deployed text can drift from the tested text.

questions.explanation: Treat prompts as code and config: review, version, evaluate, canary. Prompt registries (LangSmith, Langfuse) provide labels like production/staging.

questions.prompt: Which statements about few-shot prompting and system prompts are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Examples should cover edge cases and balanced labels, otherwise the model copies the majority pattern.
options.why: True: skewed examples bias the output.

options.text: The order of examples can change the output.
options.why: True: recency and ordering effects are well documented.

options.text: Adding more examples always improves quality, so use as many as fit.
options.why: False: returns diminish, cost and latency grow, and noisy examples can hurt.

options.text: Untrusted user text should be clearly delimited from the instructions.
options.why: True: delimiters help but do not fully stop prompt injection.

options.text: A system prompt makes it impossible for a user message to override the rules.
options.why: False: models can still be steered by injected text, so enforce rules in code too.

questions.explanation: Few-shot is cheap steering, not a guarantee. Combine delimiters, output validation and permission checks outside the model.

questions.prompt: Assume Anthropic's usual multipliers: a 5-minute cache write costs 1.25 times the base input price and a cache read costs 0.1 times. A 4,000-token prefix is written once and then read 5 times within the TTL. Counting only the prefix, how many full-price token equivalents does the bill come to?
questions.explanation: 4,000 x (1.25 + 5 x 0.1) = 4,000 x 1.75 = 7,000, against 24,000 without caching (6 x 4,000). The write premium is why caching only pays off when the prefix is reused. Newer models can have a lower read multiplier, so check the pricing page.
